newsitem.title: GERMANY: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND FORGETS SESTRIERE, ATTACKS WORLD CUP.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND FORGETS SESTRIERE, ATTACKS WORLD CUP.

text.p: France's reigning World Cup downhill champion Luc Alphand has to forget his disappointing world championships and tame one of the most dangerous mountains on the Alpine skiing circuit this weekend.
Alphand, who has won the World Cup downhill title for the last two seasons, suffered a spectacular crash at this month's championships in the Italian resort of Sestriere.

But the 31-year-old Frenchman heads for a downhill and two super giant slaloms in this German resort knowing he is in a perfect position to stamp his authority on the speed disciplines as the World Cup moves into a decisive phase.
"I have something to prove," said Alphand who is 71 points ahead of Italy's Kristian Ghedina in the downhill rankings.
"It would have been great to have got a gold medal in Italy but I still have to keep ahead in the downhill World Cup."

The steep Kandahar hill has one of the toughest pistes in skiing because the racers have very little opportunity to glide on the fast course and must work their skis hard all the way down the hill -- painful punishment for the thighs and knees.
The weather in the relatively low-altitude German resort can also be a problem and the course has often had to use artificial snow in the past.
And then there is the painful memory of former women's world champion Ulrike Maier of Austria who lost her life on the hill three years ago after a horrifying crash which shocked the skiing world.
Alphand, dubbed "Unlucky Luc" in the past because of his injury problems, has mixed memories of the resort -- a bad crash in 1992 followed by triumph last season.
The Frenchman, however, is a racer who likes to attack difficult hills.
"It is a perfect hill for me, very challenging. It's a real downhiller's course," he said. "You really have to go for it."
The downhill takes place on Saturday, sandwiched between super-Gs on Friday and Sunday.

Alphand won the last super-G before the world championships in the Swiss resort of Laax but did not make the top 10 in Sestriere, saying he was weak and fighting a cold. He also leads the super-G standings ahead of Austrian Hans Knauss.

Alphand is also just four points behind Norwegian Kjetil Andre Aamodt in the overall World Cup standings before the final 11 races of the season which include seven speed events where he has a superb chance to pick up more points.
Although he is only racing in the four super-Gs and three downhills, Alphand has an opportunity to become the first Frenchman to pick up the prestigious title since Jean-Claude Killy in 1968.
But Alphand has had enough bad luck to play down his chances.
"I'm not thinking about the overall World Cup. Aamodt has a great chance. He races in all the disciplines," he said.
